title: Holy, holy, holy (Isaiah 6:3)
hookLine: the preface ends and heaven and earth sing the same song

cards: In the year King Ozias died, the prophet Isaiah says, he saw the Lord. He is in the Temple in Jerusalem, and what he sees, nobody could paint properly.
The Lord, seated on a throne, high and elevated, the edge of his robe filling the whole Temple.
Above him stand fiery creatures called seraphim, each with six wings: two covering the face, two covering the feet, and two to fly.
They call out to each other, back and forth, so loud that the doorposts shake and the house fills with smoke. What they're calling is sung at every Mass, all over the world, today.

teach.b: Here's what they call, in the Douay-Rheims: "Holy, holy, holy, the Lord God of hosts, all the earth is full of his glory." In Latin, the first word is Sanctus, holy, and that's the name of this moment at Mass.
In Hebrew, the word is kadosh, and it means more than good or pure. It means set apart. Other.
Some readers hear in the triple repeat Hebrew's way of saying the utmost: holy beyond all holy. Here's how the Mass gets there.
After the gifts, the priest says: lift up your hearts, in Latin, Sursum corda, and the people answer that they lift them up to the Lord.
Then a prayer called the preface gives thanks, and ends by joining the angels and saints in their song. The whole church sings the seraphim's words, then adds a second line, from Palm Sunday.
When Jesus rode into Jerusalem, the crowds shouted, in the Douay-Rheims: "Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord." With Hosanna on either side.

teach.h: THE TEMPLE AND PALM SUNDAY MEET.
teach.b: So in one short song, the Temple vision and the Palm Sunday crowd meet. And this isn't a copy.

teach.h: HOLY, HOLY, HOLY, THE LORD GOD OF HOSTS.
teach.b: The church isn't imitating heaven. For a moment, Catholics believe, heaven and earth are singing the same song at the same time.

The same verse is at the heart of a prayer in the synagogue, the Kedushah, so Jewish neighbors sing it too. And in the book of Revelation, the creatures around the throne never stop singing it, day and night.

how: At the end of the preface, the whole congregation sings or says the Sanctus, joining the seraphim's words from Isaiah with the Palm Sunday Hosanna; in many churches everyone then kneels for the Eucharistic Prayer.

games.q: you're Isaiah, in the Temple. you see the Lord on a throne and seraphim crying holy until the doorposts shake. what do you say?
o: that you must build a greater temple.
that you're a man of unclean lips, and undone.
games.why: Isaiah cries that he's undone, a man of unclean lips. a seraph touches his lips with a burning coal, and then he says: here I am, send me.

practice: If you pray, say the word quietly three times, holy, holy, holy, with a slow breath between each, letting each one go a little deeper than the last.
If you don't pray, think of something in your life that feels set apart, a place, a memory, a person, something you'd take your shoes off for. Just hold it, and let it be other.

wordCard.voice: Sanctus. Latin for holy: the seraphim's song from Isaiah, sung at every Mass as heaven and earth join in. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: holy, set apart. Isaiah hears it three times.

carryVoice: Your line: heaven joins in. One song, sung in the Temple and at the altar. Day one hundred and thirteen.
